target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a federal holiday would remove the main scheduling barrier to voting for working people and students.
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably remove scheduling constraints because private employers are not required to close or give paid time off; many hourly workers in retail, food service, and similar jobs would still work, so the same time pressures would remain and low-income workers could even be disadvantaged.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday would not meaningfully change workers' real schedules because not every employer must close.
objection: Even without forcing all employers to close, a federal holiday changes the schedule people operate under in practice: schools close, many businesses reduce staffing, and polling can be run in more workable daytime windows, so the holiday still increases the number of people who can vote.

target: AG1's assumption that a federal holiday would create broad daytime availability for low-income workers.
objection: Because federal holidays do not mandate private employers to close, many low-income workers in open sectors such as retail, food service, warehouses, transportation, and pharmacies may still work normal or similar shifts, so the holiday would not eliminate the time constraint for them.

target: AG2's objection that the holiday still leaves many workers unable to vote because employers may keep them working.
objection: Voting access depends on more than whether employers give paid time off: a holiday lets election officials use holiday-available workers and set polling hours more flexibly, so many people can vote before or after shifts or during newly workable daytime hours without relying entirely on employer permission.

target: AG1's claim that election-day logistics can be expanded enough to make the holiday meaningfully useful even if employers stay open.
objection: Even with staffed polling places, the real constraint is whether workers are actually free during voting hours; many hourly employees must still work, so they would have to sacrifice wages or take unpaid time, meaning the holiday does not decouple voting from employer-provided time off.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday's effect is too weak because employers can still keep workers on the job.
objection: International evidence cuts against that skepticism: 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, which suggests that shifting elections away from ordinary weekdays can meaningfully reduce scheduling barriers rather than simply shifting the burden elsewhere.

target: AG1's reliance on international weekend/holiday election practices to show a U.S. federal holiday would help.
objection: Those international examples do not prove the U.S. holiday would work the same way, because in the U.S. private employers can still keep workers on the clock; a holiday may just replace one scheduling conflict with another, leaving the barrier largely intact for the workers most likely to lose wages.

target: AG2's assumption that school closures and childcare routines do not materially help parents vote.
objection: For many parents, especially low- and moderate-income ones, the binding constraint includes school-based obligations such as drop-off, pickup, and after-school care; a holiday closes schools and disrupts those routines, creating usable daytime availability and reducing dependence on employer permission.

target: AG1's assumption that closing schools will broadly free parents to vote.
objection: School closures do not reliably solve childcare problems because many low-income parents use daycare, Head Start, informal caregivers, or other arrangements that may not close with schools, so parents may still need unpaid time or negotiated work flexibility to vote.

target: AG2's claim that childcare disruptions are too unreliable for a holiday to matter.
objection: Many childcare arrangements are school-linked or school-based, such as after-school programs and subsidized school-facility programs, so when schools close on a holiday those arrangements often close or change too, giving a substantial share of parents a real voting window.

target: AG1's argument that changing the school/childcare calendar by itself will reliably raise turnout.
objection: Even if schools close and some childcare schedules change, that does not address the main barrier for many low-income workers: they still need paid time off or risk wage loss, so a holiday by itself is not a reliable turnout reform.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday only changes a minor school routine while leaving the core barrier untouched.
objection: A holiday affects the whole weekday coordination problem—work hours, school obligations, and childcare logistics—and therefore meaningfully shifts when many people are free to vote, rather than merely altering a minor detail.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday meaningfully expands real daytime availability for workers and students.
objection: Because private employers need not close or give paid time off, many hourly workers will still have normal shifts and still need unpaid time or employer flexibility, so the holiday does not reliably create usable daytime windows for them.

target: AG1's claim that changing the school/childcare schedule is enough to make the holiday an effective access reform.
objection: Research in the opposing position says an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other reforms, because it does not consistently remove the core barriers that keep low-income workers from voting.

target: AG1's assumption that school closure means parents will have more time to vote.
objection: Even when public schools close, many low- and moderate-income parents still face private daycare, informal caregivers, or work schedules that keep them constrained, so the holiday can shift logistics without actually creating the availability needed to vote.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday's effects are too limited to matter for turnout.
objection: A holiday addresses the broader weekday coordination bottleneck by changing school, childcare, and work routines together, and election administration can align staffing with those newly workable windows, so the reform is not as limited as claimed.
